posts.title: On Trusting the Shampoo Effect
posts.description: I recently finished Jenny Jackson’s newest novel, The Shampoo Effect . And while I netted out medium on the book itself, the metaphor for which it got its name has stuck with me. The basic definition is: if hair has already been shampooed, a second wash will lather quickly. In the book, the core group of friends are said to have discovered this metaphor in their late teens/early twenties and attributed it to various parts of their lives. For example, after a night of drinking, they might decide they want to start again in the morning because they’d get drunk way faster, seeing as they weren’t starting from zero. It’s a quick lather. But the example that really blew my mind was how our tempers and moods can be more quickly affected by people and situations we are exposed to frequently. posts.title: September & October Favorites
posts.description: My favorite season is forever tied between fall and spring. But the arrival of fall this year felt like a true rescue from the relentless heat, so she’s got an extra point—at least until April. Here are some favorites from September and October. Podcasts . One thing about me, I’m a sucker for World War II content. And the History Channel’s deep dive podcast, World War II with Tom Hanks, was everything I hoped it would be. I felt like they really took their time to give as much information as possible, but in a very palatable way. . Books I’m wholly hooked on Curtis Sittenfeld’s short stories, so You Think It, I’ll Say It was a delight! It’s so rare for me to connect with the plots and characters that I only know for a short while, but she makes them all memorable, I’ll never miss one of her collections. posts.title: We Didn’t Call it a Funeral
posts.description: My grandparents didn’t want a funeral. When my grandma died unexpectedly, my grandpa was adamant about this request, and when he died a decade later, it was still ringing in our ears. So we didn’t have a service. Didn’t gather what surely would have been hundreds of people who wanted to say goodbye, or to tell one of us—their children, grandchildren, great grandchildren—how special they were. But they didn’t have to, because I knew. Ever since I was little, I knew. And I think it will be a long time before I stop running into people who remind me. Old friends or passing acquaintances whose day was made brighter or whose path was set right just by being around my grandma and grandpa. There are people I’ve never met, and people I knew but no longer see that carry around memories of my grandma and grandpa, smiling as they think, every once in a while, they were so great. So we had a funeral. Not the big, bustling kind. Not the crowded, catered kind. And not the immediate, aftermath kind.
